newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean president signs new labour law.
newsitem.headline: South Korean president signs new labour law.

text.p: South Korea's president signed a labour bill into law on Wednesday to replace legislation that sparked a wave of strikes after it was rammed through last December, a presidential spokesman said.

Kim Young-sam, in a special message to the nation marking the introduction of the law, urged a "grand compromise" between management and labour to help improve South Korea's international competitiveness.

"On the occasion of declaring the new labour law, we must all start building the future of prosperity and abundance by establishing new labour-management relations of participation and cooperation," he said.
A government official said the law would come into force on Thursday when it is formally gazetted.
South Korean labour unions have threatened to organise strikes in protest against the new law, but economic analysts said workers had lost their appetite for industrial action.
Kim hailed the new legislation as having historic significance, but it has drawn scorn and criticism from corporate management and unions.
Parliament on Monday passed a revised version of the bill watering down key clauses, including one making layoffs easier.
The new law also allows more than one union organisation, a move that offers legitimacy to the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
Confederation spokesman Chung Sung-hee said the group would fight the law and considered organising a fresh wave of strikes. He gave no details.

The confederation spearheaded almost one month of strikes after an earlier labour bill was forced through parliament in a dawn session while opposition deputies slept. The strikes cost $3.28 billion in lost production.
It condemns as "poisonous" clauses that will allow layoffs from 1999, bring in flexible working hours immediately and permit management to replace strikers from within the company.
Analysts question the confederation's ability to pull off another nationwide strike. They said it faced an uphill battle to get any further labour law revisions.
The Federation of Korean Industries, which represents leading industrial conglomerates, said on Tuesday it would support the new law despite its drawbacks.
"The new law could damage the spirit of financial reform and slow mergers and acquisitions," federation executive Sohn Byung-doo said.
President Kim said the new legislation was particularly meaningful because ruling and opposition parties had jointly forged a single draft through cooperation before it was passed.

Industry analysts have said the law contained many ambiguous clauses and postponements as politicians hurriedly thrashed out a bill to save face after their credibility was badly damaged by a loans scandal that implicated ruling and opposition deputies.
The new law allows sackings starting in 1999 on grounds of "management emergency" only.
Analysts said this would stall reform of the over-staffed and inefficient banking sector. Mergers and acquisitions have been touted as the best way to streamline the industry.
Financial reform was given urgency by the loans-for-kickbacks scandal this year involving questionable loans to Hanbo Steel Co which collapsed in January after piling up $5.8 billion in debts.
